lead: Every network device forwards something, and the thing it forwards fixes its layer. A hub repeats raw bits, so all its ports share one collision domain. A bridge or switch reads frames and forwards them by MAC address: a port connected to a single station is that station's collision domain, while a port connected to a hub shares one collision domain with all devices on that hub. A router reads packets and forwards them by IP address between networks, and it separates broadcast domains. This is why an office uses a switch for its desks and a router to reach the Internet. The devices exist to keep local traffic local and to move only what must cross a boundary.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.5 and Chapter 1.6 to attach each device to a layer, and Chapter 1.7 for store-and-forward packets.

blocks.text: A repeater regenerates a weakened signal and sends the bit pattern onward. It reads no address. A hub is a multiport repeater. When PC 1 sends a frame into a hub, every other port receives the same bits. The hub has no table and makes no forwarding decision.

All hub ports sit in one collision domain. If two PCs transmit together, their signals overlap and the frame is damaged; Ethernet CSMA/CD makes them back off. A hub runs half duplex, so a port cannot send and receive at once. Its bandwidth is shared: four PCs on a 100 Mbit/s hub contend for the same 100 Mbit/s, not 400 Mbit/s.

A network interface card (NIC) is the host's own layer 2 hardware. It builds frames and holds the MAC address; it is not a shared network device. A wireless access point is a layer 2 bridge to the wireless medium: it forwards frames between wireless clients and the wired LAN.

A bridge joins two LAN segments and forwards frames by MAC address. A switch is a bridge with many ports and hardware forwarding. The unit it handles is the Ethernet frame; see Unit 3 for frame format. Each frame carries a source MAC address and a destination MAC address.
A switch keeps a MAC table: MAC address → port. It performs four actions:

items: Learn: when a frame arrives on port p, record its source MAC with port p. Refresh the entry if it exists.
Filter: if the destination MAC is on port p, drop the frame.
Forward: if the destination MAC is in the table and its port is not p, send the frame out only that port.
Flood: if the destination is unknown, or is the broadcast address, send the frame out every port except p. Never send it back out of p.

blocks.text: MAC table entries age out after a timeout, so a station that moves is relearned. Multicast frames are flooded like broadcast frames.

A switch port connected to a single station is that station's collision domain. A port connected to a hub shares one collision domain with all devices on that hub. By the usual exam convention every switch port counts as one collision domain: a full-duplex link has no collisions but is still counted as its own domain. A switch still has one broadcast domain: a broadcast frame floods every port. VLANs can split that broadcast domain logically; detail is in Unit 3. A bridge does the same job at smaller scale.

A router joins different networks. It receives a frame, removes the layer 2 header, reads the destination IP address, looks up the route, and sends the packet out of the chosen interface. It then builds a new frame for that hop with a new source and destination MAC address. The IP address normally stays the same from source host to destination host; the MAC header changes at every hop.

A router separates broadcast domains. It does not forward a layer 2 broadcast from one interface to another. A host sends off-LAN traffic to its default gateway, which is the router address on its own LAN. In a home box, the word gateway often means a router plus switch plus access point in one case. In general, a gateway is any device that joins two systems with different protocols.

Collision domain: the set of devices whose transmissions can collide. Broadcast domain: the set that receives a broadcast frame. By the usual exam convention every switch port counts as one collision domain; a full-duplex link has no collisions but is still counted as its own domain. In the figure, the router joins LAN 1 and LAN 2. Under Switch 1, the switch port to the hub, the hub, and PC 1, PC 2, PC 3 form one collision domain. PC 4 has its own full-duplex switch port, so a second collision domain. Switch 2 gives PC 5 and PC 6 one each. Broadcast domains: LAN 1 is one; LAN 2 is one; the router keeps them apart, so two.

figure.caption: One row per frame of the worked example: the blue cell is the port just learned as the source's MAC entry, the orange cells are the ports the frame leaves by — 3 flooded when the destination is unknown, 1 forwarded when it is already in the table. After frame 4 the table holds A on 1, B on 2, C on 3.

spec.title: Switch MAC table after each frame (ports 1–4)
spec.aria: A 4-port switch MAC table shown after each of four frames: frame 1 learns A on port 1 and floods to ports 2, 3 and 4; frame 2 learns B on port 2 and forwards only to port 1; frame 3 floods again to ports 2, 3 and 4; frame 4 learns C on port 3 and forwards only to port 1, leaving the final table A on 1, B on 2, C on 3.

examples.question: A four-port switch starts with an empty MAC table. Ports are 1, 2, 3, 4. Frames arrive in this order: (1) A to B on port 1; (2) B to A on port 2; (3) A to C on port 1; (4) C to A on port 3. Fill the MAC table and state where each frame is sent. Give the number of ports flooded or forwarded at each step.
steps: Frame 1: source A on port 1, so learn A→1. Destination B is unknown, so flood to ports 2, 3, 4. Flooded ports = 3. Table: A→1.
Frame 2: source B on port 2, so learn B→2. Destination A is known on port 1, so forward to port 1 only. Forwarded ports = 1. Table: A→1, B→2.
Frame 3: source A on port 1; A is already on 1. Destination C is unknown, so flood to ports 2, 3, 4; never back out of port 1. Flooded ports = 3. Table unchanged.
Frame 4: source C on port 3, so learn C→3. Destination A is known on port 1, so forward to port 1 only. Forwarded ports = 1. Final table: A→1, B→2, C→3.
examples.answer: Frame 1 floods to 3 ports, frame 2 forwards to 1 port, frame 3 floods to 3 ports, frame 4 forwards to 1 port; final MAC table A on 1, B on 2, C on 3.

traps: A switch separates collision domains, not broadcast domains. A broadcast frame still floods every port in the VLAN until a router or VLAN boundary stops it.
A hub does not give each port 100 Mbit/s. All ports share one half-duplex collision domain.
A router forwards by IP address and writes a new MAC header for each hop; the source and destination IP addresses normally do not change.
A bridge and a switch work at layer 2. A switch is a multiport bridge, not a layer 3 router.
On a full-duplex switch port there are no collisions, but by the usual exam convention the port still counts as its own collision domain; do not merge it with a shared wire.

quiz.q: At which OSI layer does a hub work, and what does it forward?
quiz.a: Layer 1. It repeats raw bits and reads no address.

quiz.q: What does a switch learn from an incoming frame?
quiz.a: It learns the source MAC address and the port on which the frame arrived.

quiz.q: Why does a switch flood a frame whose destination MAC is unknown?
quiz.a: The switch has no table entry telling it which port leads to that destination, so it sends the frame out every other port to reach the host.

quiz.q: A switch table has A on port 1 and B on port 2. A frame C→A arrives on port 3. What does the switch do?
quiz.a: Learn C on port 3. A is known on port 1, so forward the frame to port 1 only.

quiz.q: Four PCs connect to one 100 Mbit/s hub and all try to send at once. What shared rate and duplex do they get?
quiz.a: They share 100 Mbit/s in one collision domain, half duplex; they do not get 100 Mbit/s each.

quiz.q: Why does replacing a hub by a switch improve throughput even when the link speed stays the same?
quiz.a: A switch port connected to a single station is that station's collision domain; a port connected to a hub shares one collision domain with all devices on that hub. So with stations on separate ports, each has its own collision domain and can run full duplex, and different ports send at the same time instead of contending for one shared hub segment. The broadcast domain is still one.

quiz.q: A broadcast frame arrives at a switch. Which ports receive it, and does a router stop it?
quiz.a: The switch floods it out every other port in the same VLAN. A router does not forward a layer 2 broadcast to another interface, so it stops the broadcast at that boundary.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern data-centre switches run programmable pipelines and are often managed by software-defined networking controllers. Whitebox switches separate the forwarding hardware from the network operating system. Wireless access points are commonly managed by a controller that pushes configuration to many units. Home gateways bundle router, switch, access point and firewall into one box. Search next for software-defined networking, OpenFlow, and whitebox switching.
